examShortTricks: Trick 1: Three preparations to memorise — reduction: RX + 2H → RH + HX (Zn/HCl, LiAlH4); Wurtz: 2RX + 2Na → R–R + 2NaX (dry ether); decarboxylation: RCOONa + NaOH(CaO) → RH + Na2CO3 (soda lime).
Trick 2: Wurtz product rule: two different halides give a MIXTURE of three alkanes — quote as the limitation when asked why Wurtz is unsuitable for unsymmetrical alkanes.
Trick 3: Kolbe electrolysis of sodium acetate gives ETHANE: 2CH3COO− → C2H6 + 2CO2 (at anode) — one equation, one mark.
keyPoints: Haloalkanes reduce to alkanes with Zn/HCl or LiAlH4.
Wurtz reaction couples two haloalkanes with dry sodium in ether.
Soda-lime decarboxylation of sodium carboxylates gives alkanes.
Kolbe electrolysis of acetate yields ethane at the anode.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write the Wurtz reaction for propane preparation. (2 marks) — C2H5Br + CH3Br... actually use 1-bromopropane: 2C3H7Br + 2Na → C6H14 + 2NaBr (dry ether).
Q. Why does Wurtz reaction give poor yields with mixed halides? (1 mark) — three possible coupling products form in a mixture.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Conditions are the marks — halogenation needs sunlight/heat (free-radical chain); nitration needs 400–500 °C vapour phase (CH4 + HNO3 → CH3NO2); sulphonation needs fuming H2SO4, long-chain alkanes only.
Trick 2: Halogenation order of ease: F2 (explosive) > Cl2 > Br2 > I2 (reversible, needs oxidant) — explain via bond energies.
Trick 3: Free-radical mechanism three steps: initiation (Cl2 → 2Cl·), propagation (Cl· + CH4 → CH3· + HCl), termination (coupling) — name the steps for the 3-mark answer.
keyPoints: Alkanes undergo free-radical substitution in sunlight.
Nitration (vapour phase, 400–500 °C) gives nitroalkanes.
Sulphonation applies to higher alkanes with fuming H2SO4.
Reactivity of halogens: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write the chlorination of methane in sunlight with mechanism type. (2 marks) — CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl; free-radical substitution.
Q. Why is iodination reversible? (1 mark) — HI formed reduces the iodide back; needs HNO3/HgO to remove HI.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Dehydration: C2H5OH —(conc. H2SO4, 170 °C)→ C2H4 + H2O; dehydrohalogenation: C2H5Br + KOH(alcoholic) → C2H4 + KBr + H2O — 'alcoholic KOH' vs 'aqueous KOH' decides alkene vs alcohol.
Trick 2: Saytzeff rule for the 2-mark extra: elimination removes H from the β-carbon with FEWER hydrogens → more substituted (stable) alkene predominates.
Trick 3: Partial hydrogenation: RC≡CR + H2 (Lindlar/Pd–BaSO4) → cis-alkene; full reduction gives alkane.
keyPoints: Alcohols dehydrate with conc. H2SO4 or Al2O3 at high temperature.
Alcoholic KOH removes HX from haloalkanes (β-elimination).
Saytzeff: the more substituted alkene is the major product.
Catalytic partial hydrogenation of alkynes gives alkenes.
practiceQuestions: Q. Prepare ethene from ethanol and from bromoethane. (2 marks) — dehydration (conc. H2SO4, 170 °C); dehydrohalogenation (alc. KOH).
Q. Why is aqueous KOH not used for alkene preparation? (1 mark) — it gives substitution (alcohol) instead of elimination.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Markovnikov one line: H goes to the carbon with MORE hydrogens (rich get richer); propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane. Reason: more stable secondary carbocation.
Trick 2: Peroxide effect (Kharasch) applies to HBr ONLY: Br adds to the less substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov) via free-radical chain — HCl/HI do not show it.
Trick 3: Addition order of reactivity of HX: HI > HBr > HCl (bond strength falls) — a favourite 1-marker.
keyPoints: Markovnikov's rule: the negative part of the addendum attaches to the carbon with fewer hydrogens.
Reason: stability of the intermediate carbocation.
Peroxide (Kharasch) effect: HBr adds anti-Markovnikov by a free-radical mechanism.
Alkenes also add H2 (Ni), X2, HX, H2O (hydration).
practiceQuestions: Q. Predict the product of propene + HBr with and without peroxide. (2 marks) — 2-bromopropane (Markovnikov); 1-bromopropane (peroxide effect).
Q. Why does the peroxide effect not operate with HCl? (1 mark) — H–Cl bond is too strong for the propagation step's exothermic requirement.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Four routes: C + H2 (electric arc, 2700 °C) → C2H2; vic-dihalide + 2 alc. KOH → alkyne (double dehydrohalogenation); CHCl3 + 2Ag (heat) → C2H2 + 2AgCl; CHI3 + 4Ag → C2H2.
Trick 2: Double dehydrohalogenation needs TWO equivalents of base and gives the terminal alkyne; the first elimination gives the vinyl halide.
Trick 3: Ethyne from CaC2 + H2O → C2H2 + Ca(OH)2 — the industrial/lab route; quote 'carbide route' for the mark.
keyPoints: Ethyne is prepared from calcium carbide and water.
Vicinal dihalides lose two HX with alcoholic KOH to give alkynes.
Chloroform/iodoform with heated silver powder gives ethyne.
Direct union of carbon and hydrogen needs an electric arc.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write the preparation of ethyne from 1,2-dibromoethane. (2 marks) — CH2BrCH2Br + 2KOH(alc.) → C2H2 + 2KBr + 2H2O.
Q. Give the industrial preparation of ethyne. (1 mark) — CaC2 + 2H2O → C2H2 + Ca(OH)2.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Addition goes in TWO stages: alkyne → alkene → alkane; with HX follow Markovnikov (vinyl → ethylidene halide).
Trick 2: Hydration with dilute H2SO4/HgSO4: ethyne → acetaldehyde (via enol tautomerisation); other alkynes → ketones — the enol–keto line earns the mark.
Trick 3: Acidic nature tests (terminal alkynes only): Na metal → sodium acetylide + H2; ammoniacal AgNO3 → white Ag2C2; ammoniacal Cu2Cl2 → red Cu2C2 — three colours to memorise.
Trick 4: Acidic reason: sp-carbon (50% s-character) holds the electron pair closer to the nucleus.
keyPoints: Alkynes add H2, X2, HX, H2O in two steps.
Hydration of ethyne gives acetaldehyde (Kucherov reaction).
Terminal alkynes are weakly acidic (sp C–H) and form acetylides with Na, Ag and Cu salts.
sp carbon's 50% s-character explains the acidity.
practiceQuestions: Q. How will you distinguish ethyne from ethene? (2 marks) — ethyne gives white ppt with ammoniacal AgNO3; ethene does not.
Q. Why are terminal alkynes acidic? (1 mark) — high s-character of sp carbon stabilises the acetylide anion.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Two tests, two decolourisations — bromine water (red-brown → colourless) and Baeyer's reagent (alkaline KMnO4, purple → colourless with brown MnO2).
Trick 2: Both tests are also passed by aldehydes/phenols — add 'and no reaction with saturated hydrocarbons' to make the test conclusive.
Trick 3: Distinguishing ethene vs ethyne: ammoniacal AgNO3/Cu2Cl2 precipitate only with ethyne.
keyPoints: Unsaturated compounds decolourise bromine water without HBr evolution.
Baeyer's test: cold dilute alkaline KMnO4 decolourised with brown MnO2 (diol formed).
Saturated hydrocarbons fail both tests.
Terminal alkynes additionally form metal acetylides.
practiceQuestions: Q. Give Baeyer's test for unsaturation with observation. (2 marks) — purple KMnO4 decolourises; brown MnO2 precipitates; glycol forms.
Q. Which reagent distinguishes ethene from ethyne? (1 mark) — ammoniacal AgNO3 (white ppt with ethyne only).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: State/solubility common row: first four members are gases, next are liquids; all are non-polar, insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents — one row covers three classes.
Trick 2: Boiling point rises with carbon number; for the SAME carbon number: alkyne > alkene > alkane (more linear packing/s-polarity) — the subtle mark.
Trick 3: Odour fact: ethene sweet smell, ethyne garlic-like — quick identification line.
keyPoints: C1–C4 hydrocarbons are gases; C5–C17 liquids; higher are solids.
All three classes are non-polar and water-insoluble.
Boiling points increase with chain length; alkynes slightly higher than alkenes/alkanes of equal carbon count.
Density increases with molecular mass but stays below water.
practiceQuestions: Q. Compare the boiling points of ethane, ethene and ethyne. (2 marks) — ethyne > ethene > ethane; increasing s-character and linearity.
Q. Why are alkanes insoluble in water? (1 mark) — non-polar molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds with water.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Electrode logic: hydrocarbon forms at the ANODE (oxidation of carboxylate), H2 at cathode — stating the electrode earns the first mark.
Trick 2: Three recipes — sodium acetate → ethane; sodium succinate → ethene (plus CO2); sodium fumarate/maleate → ethyne.
Trick 3: General anode reaction: 2RCOO− − 2e → R–R + 2CO2; remember CO2 bubbles as the visible observation.
keyPoints: Kolbe electrolysis: concentrated sodium carboxylate solution electrolysed.
Alkane forms at the anode: 2RCOO− → R–R + 2CO2 + 2e.
Sodium succinate gives ethene; sodium fumarate gives ethyne.
Hydrogen is liberated at the cathode.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write the electrode reactions for the Kolbe electrolysis of sodium acetate. (3 marks) — anode: 2CH3COO− → C2H6 + 2CO2 + 2e; cathode: 2H2O + 2e → H2 + 2OH−.
Q. Which salt gives ethene by Kolbe's method? (1 mark) — sodium succinate.
